This study demonstrated that with open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing, field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries is now feasible without well-resourced agencies. It produced high-accuracy, 30-meter cropland extent maps for Australia and China.
Cropland is defined by what it does over time as well as by its appearance on a single date. Maps of cropland often disagree with one another, use coarse satellite pixels, or depend on national statistics that arrive late and vary in quality. Better maps give decision-makers a clearer, more consistent picture of the land. Knowing the footprint of cropland helps estimate irrigation demand, assess pressure on river basins and aquifers, and target water management. Estimating food production requires knowing how much land is cultivated and where.
Cropland maps typically do not say which crops are grown, whether land is irrigated, or how intensively it is farmed. That information comes from crop-type and irrigation mapping, which build on the same foundation.
Landsat-8 offers 30-meter pixels, fine enough to resolve individual fields in many agricultural areas. It revisits each location about every 16 days. Repeated mapping over time reveals cropland expansion, abandonment, and conversion to urban use. Observations were composited into summaries capturing seasonal vegetation patterns, including cropland's characteristic rise and fall in greenness.
At 30 meters, a single pixel can contain a mix of crops, fallow land, trees, roads, and buildings. Pixel mixing makes cropland extent hard to determine where fields are small, such as much of China.
The study used Landsat-8 imagery, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE). GEE hosts the Landsat archive alongside other datasets and runs computation on Google's cloud infrastructure. In GEE, analysis can be written once and executed across enormous areas without moving the data. Compositing, feature extraction, classification, and accuracy assessment can all happen in GEE.

Our Cities, Our Future
Where many of our cities are growing
Much urban growth happens in peri-urban slums. These overcrowded, under-served neighborhoods feature cramped housing, poor sanitation, and stretched or absent public services. Their narrow lanes also double as playgrounds, exposing unsupervised children to traffic, polluted water, abuse, and exploitation. These are the neighborhoods we’re working in.
A Kampala-based organization working in these communities has proposed free, safe, community-run resource centers. The plan is a network of community resource centers built inside or next to the neighborhoods they serve. These centers would let poor and orphaned children play, learn, eat, and get basic health care.
Open channels of drainage run past doorways. Caregivers work long hours or are away from home, so young children are often unsupervised. Orphans and children from the most fragile households may have no reliable adult to watch over them. The proposal insists on community ownership, with centers meant to belong to the neighborhood. Parents, guardians, local leaders, and youth help plan, run, and oversee each center. Local government and community structures align the centers with public services and child-protection systems. Where possible, caregivers and volunteers come from the surrounding area, creating jobs and building trust.
The proposal is ambitious, aiming to break the cycle at several points at once. But it’s also built on partnerships. We’re asking you to join us in making it happen. Here’s how:
- We need financial support to open the first centers. Then we can rely on a network of partners to extend what each center can do.
- We need organizations, faith-based groups, and businesses to provide expertise, materials, training opportunities, and funding.
- We need schools and educators to support learning and ease the transition into formal education.
- We need NGOs and faith-based groups to provide health facilities and practitioners who can offer referrals, outreach clinics, and maternal health services.
- We need you to share our vision, partner by offering services, expertise, or resources, and support the work financially.

What is a border collie?
Border collies are working dogs that have been bred for herding. They are brilliant, but their intelligence comes at a price. The breed’s herding precision has been shaped over centuries in hard country by people who needed working dogs. Early dogs were regional working collies, not a standardized breed. Early breeding was careful selection by working shepherds with performance as the only measure. Early dogs were valued for stamina, intelligence, and an instinct to gather and control stock. They were not a standardized breed, but they were regional working collies. A dog that could herd was bred. Appearance did not save a dog that couldn’t herd. A dog that tired quickly, panicked easily, or needed constant direction was a liability. Dogs that thought independently, endured bad weather, and read animal movement earned their keep and passed on their traits. Later, sheepdog trials began in the 19th century and remain popular. Trials let shepherds compare dogs side by side and rewarded dogs that moved stock calmly and efficiently under pressure. The borderlands between England and Scotland in the 17th through 19th centuries was rough, hilly terrain where sheep were a livelihood. Drovers moved livestock over long distances to markets. Shepherds tended flocks across open hillsides where a straying animal could mean real loss. The breed’s origins lie in these borderlands. The variety in appearance reflects breeders who cared above all about ability. A dog’s appearance didn’t save a dog that couldn’t herd. Adam Telfer was a Northumberland shepherd working in the 19th century. Telfer is often credited with helping consolidate the border collie type through deliberate crossbreeding. But his contribution was fixing working traits so they reappeared reliably in each generation, not creating a particular look. Telfer’s line of dogs was prized for ability and consistency. Descendants of Telfer’s dogs became the foundation of the modern breed, and later celebrated herding dogs trace back to this lineage. Historical accounts of early breeding are patchy, so finer details should be held loosely. Later, the border collie was shaped by a working-over-looks ethos, unlike many breeds refined around a show-ring standard. Our Curriculum
The Diocese of Richmond's Consensus Curriculum is a framework for our Catholic schools. It spans the disciplines of an elementary and middle school program, placing significant trust in our teachers. We ask them to be both skilled and faithful, so that students learn from how a teacher treats a struggling classmate, how they handle a conflict, or how they respond to a hard question. The teacher’s example is part of the curriculum in a Catholic school.
Our Catholic worldview shapes how students approach literature, history, science, and the arts. Faith is the lens through which we teach every subject in the Consensus Curriculum. We have confidence in the Church’s teaching that parents are the primary educators of their children, and that our schools are there to support, not replace, that role. The Benziger Family Life Series is a program associated with the curriculum that addresses human growth, relationships, and family life from a Catholic perspective. Its purpose is to support parents, not replace them. Families should check with their school about how it communicates with parents and handles questions about family life content.
As spiritual leaders, principals shape a school culture where prayer, sacraments, service, and Catholic identity are lived realities. But they also serve as both instructional leader and spiritual leader of the school community, ensuring that the curriculum is implemented, observing classrooms, supporting teachers’ professional growth, reviewing student progress, and seeing that standards translate into real learning.
Teachers find natural, honest connections between subject matter and faith, and the material is framed by Catholic teaching on the dignity of the human person and the goodness of the body as created by God. Consistency gives families confidence that a child moving between Catholic schools in the diocese will meet a recognizable standard. This small Perthshire town is much older than the dukedom, but the Atholl family was a powerful presence in the district when the bridge was built. Their influence over the town grew as old church structures lost authority. Much of the land and property around the cathedral came under their control over time, and the estate shaped the street layout, the setting of the cathedral and the wider landscape around the town. The estate also provided work in forestry, farming and property maintenance, and supported local institutions.
The Murrays had held land across this part of Perthshire for centuries, but after the Reformation the cathedral fell into partial ruin. The choir remained in use as the parish church, while the ruined nave stood beside it. The estate's stewardship of the cathedral grounds helped preserve this important site, and over the following decades the town was rebuilt.
The centre of Dunkeld is marked by whitewashed cottages with neat gables and a cathedral by the water. Towns like Dunkeld historically relied on wells, springs and the river for water, which was carried by hand and of uncertain quality. The water running to Dunkeld's homes was a gift of the Atholl estate, and the people of Dunkeld recognised this as a practical improvement to daily life. They marked this gift in stone, a stone fountain standing in the middle of Dunkeld's square.
This fountain dates from 1866, and commemorates George Murray, 6th Duke of Atholl, who died in 1864. The people of Dunkeld chose a fountain, a structure that delivers water, as the memorial to the Duke instead of a statue. The 6th Duke's great act of public service to Dunkeld was bringing piped water to the town, one of the most significant improvements a Victorian community could receive, reducing drudgery and risk of disease. The 4th Duke of Atholl is known as the "Planter Duke", planting vast numbers of larches and other conifers across Atholl lands. The plantations transformed the look of the hills, and became part of the area's identity, drawing walkers and visitors to this day. The woodlands around Dunkeld still bear the mark of these plantings.

After the Battle of Killiecrankie in 1689, Jacobite Highlanders and the Cameronian regiment fought in Dunkeld, and much of the town burned. The town was rebuilt over the following decades. Our modern homes use paper for everything: grocery lists, to-do lists, phone messages, reminders and more. They’re used for a few hours then thrown away. The result? A steady stream of waste and a steady drain on money. Here are some easy, eco-friendly household swaps that can mean less trash, cleaner waterways, less wasted food and more money.
Start with paper towels, disposable wipes and single-use spray bottles. Replace them with washable mop pads, microfiber cloths that can replace most paper towels and trap dust and grime well (often with just water!), and refillable spray bottles filled with concentrated cleaners or refill pouches. You can keep a roll of paper towels on hand for truly messy jobs; the goal is to cut back. A pack of microfiber cloths costs about the same as a few rolls of paper towels and can be used for years. It will last longer if you have a small basket under the sink to keep your used cloths in, so they can go in with the regular laundry. These cloths can trap dust and grime well and can be machine-washed many times.
Next, consider sticky notes. Most are not easily recyclable because of their adhesive. Use a dry-erase board in a central place — the fridge, entryway or home office — to replace them and all the scrap paper you use for grocery lists, to-do lists, phone messages and reminders. You’ll buy far fewer notepads and sticky-note packs. A shared board also helps a household stay organized by showing what is needed from the store and what’s happening this week. Photographing the grocery list before you leave will eliminate the need for a paper copy.
There’s a lot of battery usage in your house. They’re used in remotes, game controllers, wireless mice, kids’ toys, flashlights and smoke detectors. Disposable batteries are used once and usually end up in the trash. Rechargeable batteries cost more upfront, but in frequently used devices, they often pay for themselves after a handful of charges. Modern “low self-discharge” nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) batteries hold their charge for months in a drawer and work in low-drain devices. A single rechargeable battery can be reused hundreds of times, replacing a pile of disposables.
Batteries contain metals that take energy to mine and process. If they’re not disposed of properly, they can leach harmful materials. If you’re using disposable batteries, make sure to recycle them. Rechargeable nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) batteries plus a charger can replace disposables.
The next big thing is to tackle food waste. It’s one of the biggest household contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. Shopping locally and seasonally often means less packaging, less time in refrigerated storage and less spoilage before it gets to the buyer, which means fresher produce that lasts longer at home and less wasted dollars in the trash. Start with one weekly item you buy locally, such as eggs, apples or summer tomatoes, and build from there. You don’t have to shop exclusively at farmers’ markets to make a difference — shift a part of your grocery habits to local, in-season food and you’ll enjoy the benefits. Food that lasts longer means fewer wasted dollars in the trash. In-season produce is often cheaper because there is plenty of it, and seasonal produce is often cheaper because it’s plentiful.
Next, let’s look at the car wash. Washing your car in your driveway sends water, soap, brake dust, oil and road grime into the storm drain. In many areas, storm drains carry runoff untreated to local streams, rivers and lakes. Commercial car washes are generally required to send their wastewater to treatment facilities rather than storm drains, and many use high-pressure, low-volume equipment and water reclamation systems, using much less fresh water per car than a typical home wash. A basic automatic car wash is often inexpensive, especially with a membership or multi-wash pass. Choose a car wash that’s on your route already, such as near the grocery store or gym, so it fits in with your errands. If you can, try to go to a car wash that recycles its water.
Last, consider the dry erase board. That one dry-erase board can replace thousands of sheets of paper over its lifetime. No more buying notepads and sticky-note packs. No more sheets of paper for grocery lists, to-do lists, phone messages and reminders. No more waste. And there you have it. Together, these swaps mean less trash, cleaner waterways, less wasted food and more money.
Try tackling one swap per week and add another once it feels automatic. If you feel like you need more, try starting with one swap per week and add another once it feels automatic. In no time, you’ll have a cleaner home and a lighter footprint.

Warehouses are where goods wait. Waiting costs money, so warehouses are tools, worth keeping only if they do a job. But many executives treat warehouses as a given, like loading docks or invoices. They need to remember that warehouses are tools, and apply the framework repeatedly, rather than a one-time audit.
The classic functions of a warehouse cover most legitimate reasons to have one: break-bulk, storage, consolidation, and value-added customization. Information provision is another reason, but it works best as a supporting argument, because systems can usually provide it without buildings. The four classic functions cover most legitimate reasons to have a warehouse:
- Break-bulk: A warehouse that receives bulk shipments and splits them into smaller orders is performing a break-bulk function. A non-profit organization supplied office products to its member agencies: paper, pens, toner, folders, and similar staples. The center failed this test because the goods arrived in customer-ready quantities. The office-supplies center failed the break-bulk test because goods arrived in customer-ready quantities.
- Storage: Storage lets supply and demand operate on different rhythms. Seasonal products, long production runs, and uncertain demand justify holding inventory close to the customer. But the non-profit ran its own distribution center to serve the agencies. The center failed this test because demand was stable and predictable.
- Consolidation: A warehouse that gathers goods from many suppliers and combines them into one shipment for the customer is the reverse of break-bulk. It can reduce freight costs and the number of deliveries a customer must receive and process. The center failed this test because combining goods gave no meaningful freight savings.
- Customization: Some warehouses label, kit, package, assemble, or configure products to customer needs, often delaying final differentiation until the last responsible moment. This can reduce the risk of holding the wrong variety of product, or make it cheaper or more flexible to do the work close to the customer than at the factory. The office-supplies center failed this test because there was no on-site value-added work.
- Information: Warehouses can provide accurate inventory visibility, order status, demand signals, and tracking. But information is the weakest argument for a warehouse on its own, because systems can usually provide it without buildings. The information function was not needed on its own, because order tracking could run through suppliers or software. The information test: would the information still be available, at similar quality, if the building disappeared.
A distribution center that only receives, stores, and reships goods that could have gone straight to the customer is a detour. A distribution center that earned its place ten years ago may not today. A facility that fails every test is overhead, not a strategic asset. The sensible answer for the case was elimination: have suppliers ship directly to agencies, or use a distributor that already offers consolidated delivery. Agencies received the same products they could have received directly from the supplier, but later and at higher cost.
Many executives treat warehouses as a given, like loading docks or invoices. But they are where goods wait, and waiting costs money. Warehouses are tools, worth keeping only if they do a job. Start from function: ask what the facility does that would not happen otherwise. “We have always done it this way” is a warning.
- Break-bulk: does the customer need smaller quantities than the supplier ships, and is it cheaper to move the bulk to one point first. Example: suppliers ship products to a center, the center stores them, and staff pick orders and ship them to the agencies. The center adds a handling step: every item is received, put away, picked, packed, and shipped a second time. Each additional handling step adds cost and delay. Example: suppliers already pack office goods in the quantities agencies buy, so nothing needs to be broken down into smaller lots. This collection summarises approaches to inclusion in six regions: Australia, Canada, Europe, Africa, Bangladesh, and New Zealand. It is designed to serve as a discussion prompt for people in policy, education, community development, or philanthropy. Pick one region and read its key policy documents and community reports. Ask how its lessons apply to your own context.
Australia
Most of the practical work for inclusion in Australia is happening in local communities. Initiatives led by people from the communities they aim to serve allow new arrivals to see themselves in leadership roles. Workplace initiatives that recognise overseas qualifications and offer bridging pathways avoid entry-level resets.
In education, there is a strong emphasis on community-based responses to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission findings that work well, particularly in education and child welfare. Grassroots peace committees, community radio, and youth dialogue forums are important tools for reducing stigma and preventing conflict. Civil society and community programs document land rights and support local advocacy.
Canada
Canada was among the first countries to make multiculturalism official policy. The Canadian Multiculturalism Act (1988) remains a worldwide reference point. Key lessons from relations with First Nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples, and from the gap between immigration targets and actual economic integration, come from the following:

High blood pressure is called “the silent killer” for a reason: it usually causes no pain, dizziness, or obvious warning. It’s only after years of wear and tear that the damage shows up—straining the heart and damaging arteries, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, and heart failure.
While high blood pressure (hypertension) may sound scary, measuring blood pressure is one of the simplest first steps toward preventing cardiovascular disease. That’s why the American Heart Association recommends checking blood pressure at home if you’ve been diagnosed with high blood pressure or if your doctor has asked you to do so.
Home monitoring is an easy, practical way to find out how your blood pressure behaves across ordinary days away from the stress of the clinic. It can help you and your doctor spot risk factors years before they cause harm.
But blood pressure tends to surge in the morning, and that surge is linked to cardiovascular events. So, how often should you check your blood pressure at home? There’s no one right answer. The frequency is up to you and your healthcare provider, and the right target for you is unique.
Still, there are some guidelines to consider. If you’ve been diagnosed with high blood pressure or your doctor has asked you to monitor at home, take readings for about seven days before your next medical appointment or after a medication change.
If you’re an adult without a diagnosis, especially if you’re over 40 or have risk factors such as family history, diabetes, excess weight, or kidney disease, occasional home checks can benefit you, too. One week of readings every few months, or whenever a clinic reading is high, is a reasonable approach for proactive adults.
Many guidelines suggest discarding the first day’s results and averaging the rest, but a full week of readings will give you a more reliable baseline that’s more informative than any single number.
For both diagnosed high blood pressure and doctor-requested monitoring, try measuring twice a day, morning and evening, with two readings each time, one minute apart. Record both with the date and time.
Most automatic upper-arm monitors are generally more accurate than wrist or finger devices, but even the best device can give misleading results if you don’t use it correctly. There are several things that can make a good device give misleading results.
The most overlooked source of error is cuff size. A cuff that is too large can read low, while a cuff that is too small will give falsely high readings. To check the size, measure around the middle of your upper arm and compare with the size range printed on the cuff or in the manual.
When in doubt, use the smaller size. Most devices come with a standard cuff, but larger or smaller sizes are sold separately.
A rolled-up sleeve should not act as a tourniquet. Place the cuff on bare skin, not over clothing. Rest your arm on a table or desk so the middle of the cuff is at heart level. Keep your arm relaxed and supported by the table, with your palm facing upward.
Place both feet flat on the floor with your legs uncrossed. Sit quietly for at least five minutes before measuring, without talking, scrolling your phone, or watching something stressful. An arm hanging below heart level will give a falsely high reading, while an arm raised above heart level will give a falsely low reading.
Measure at the same times each day so your readings are comparable. Take two readings one minute apart and record both with the date and time. Morning measurement: within an hour of waking, after you’ve used the bathroom, before eating, drinking coffee, exercising, or taking your blood pressure medication.
Evening measurement: before dinner or before bed, at roughly the same time each day. Wait at least 30 minutes after caffeine, smoking, exercise, or alcohol before measuring. Stay still and quiet while the device inflates. Rest the arm on a table or desk.
Keep in mind that pain, rushing, or being upset can temporarily push your numbers up. So, if you get a very high reading without any symptoms, rest five minutes and measure again. If it’s still that high, contact your doctor promptly.
A reading of 180/120 or higher, especially if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, weakness, or difficulty speaking, is a reason to seek urgent medical attention. If you’re fine, empty your bladder before measuring—your full bladder can raise the reading.
A single doctor’s office reading is only a snapshot. It’s just a single number out of the day. Blood pressure naturally rises and falls throughout the day, so patterns matter more than individual readings. That’s why measuring blood pressure at home is so useful.
Home readings help only if the numbers are accurate. Setup errors can make a good device give misleading results. For a very high reading without symptoms, rest five minutes and measure again. If still that high, contact your doctor promptly.
Don’t diagnose or adjust medication on your own. Bring your log to your appointment so the clinician can see the full pattern. The targets will vary by individual, but home readings averaging 130/80 or higher are generally considered elevated enough to discuss with a doctor.
Once your blood pressure is well controlled and stable, many people check a few times a week or do a one-week round about monthly. But don’t check constantly. Checking constantly can fuel anxiety and lead you to overreact to normal fluctuations.
You can keep track of your blood pressure readings in a notebook, spreadsheet, or app. They all work. Once you’re set up, measuring your blood pressure at home takes only a few minutes. It can reveal a risk factor years before it causes harm. And that’s worth the effort.

This year, the United Nations has declared 2019 to be the International Year of the Periodic Table of Chemical Elements (IYPT 2019) to celebrate the centennial of the founding of the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) and the 150th anniversary of Russian scientist Dmitri Mendeleev’s discovery of the relationships underlying the Periodic Table. The Periodic Table brings order to the chaos of the physical world and is both a reference tool and a research tool, significant across almost every scientific discipline.
The symposium to be held in February will address how much female researchers have contributed to the content of the contemporary Periodic Table. It will take place in collaboration with IUPAC, the International Union of the History and Philosophy of Science, the European Chemical Society, Real Sociedad Española de Química, and the University of Murcia, and will feature presentations on the past, present, and future of the Periodic Table. The opening ceremony will include a lecture by Dutch chemist Ben Feringa, winner of the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
IUPAC oversees a wide array of scientific nomenclature and is the de facto keeper of the Periodic Table. It keeps the Periodic Table as up-to-date and accurate as current science allows. Animated on-line versions of the Periodic Table make it user friendly, and there are a number of musical versions, including one set to music.
As part of its activities celebrating IYPT 2019, the Chemical Institute of Canada (CIC) has been offered a number of keepsakes from the ElemenTree model, developed by the late Fernando Dufour, a professor at Collège Ahuntsic in Montreal. The CIC will announce in 2019 how its members can obtain a copy of this physical representation of the Periodic Table, along with more announcements about its IYPT 2019 celebrations.

This is a discussion of MOA (minute of angle) and its significance in rifle scope adjustments and the use of MOA in describing rifle precision. Many shooters will find this helpful in their quest to better understand and improve their accuracy.
This will be a rather long discussion, and it will cover some basic math and science, so grab a cup of coffee and read on!
What is MOA?
MOA is the abbreviation for Minute of Angle, and is part of mathematics, described as our only universal language. It is used as the basis for firearm sighting scopes to make adjustments to the point of impact (POI) of the projectile.
The word 'minute' in MOA refers to one minute of a degree, not a minute of time, and a degree is one of 360 degrees of arc in a full circle. Therefore, a full circle is 360 degrees of arc and each degree has 60 minutes of arc. Each minute of arc represents 0.1047 / 60 = 0.001745 inch at 6 inches from the center.
To put that into a simple example, let's take a circle with a 6 inch radius. The circumference of that circle is (6 x 2) x 3.1416 = 37.6992 inches. The symbol (") is inaccurate for inches in this context and misleading because it also represents 'second of angle' (1/60 of a minute of angle), so I'll use (') to represent minute of angle.
So, we have a circle with a 6 inch radius that has a circumference of 37.6992 inches. We have a distance of 6 inches from the center of the circle, and each minute of arc represents 0.1047 / 60 = 0.001745 inch. So, one degree of arc represents 0.1047 / 360 = 0.00029 inch at 6 inches from the center.
A full circle has 360 degrees of arc, so that's 360 x 0.00029 = 0.1047 inch at 6 inches from the center. One degree covers 37.6992 / 360 = 0.1047 inch at 6 inches from the center.
Expressing Precision in MOA
The use of MOA to express precision is more concise since no distance is included. All that is required is the angle measure to calculate it at other distances. MOA value at 50 yards is 1/2 the 100 yard value; 70% at 70 yards; twice at 200 yards; 6 times at 600 yards, and so on. It's very simple!
In metric countries 27.77 mm @ 100 meters is used to keep the same proportion as 1 MOA = 1.000 inch @ 100 yards. The real difference between inch and MOA is 0.47 inch at 1000 yards.

For most shooters, this is really all that is necessary to know about MOA. But, for those who want to go a bit deeper, I'll continue.
The use of MOA in firearm sighting scopes is actually a rather complex matter. The math behind MOA is fairly simple, but the application to firearm sighting scopes is more complex.
To understand why, let's look at the MOA math. If we take a circle with a 6 inch radius, the circumference of that circle is (6 x 2) x 3.1416 = 37.6992 inches. The symbol (") is inaccurate for inches in this context and misleading because it also represents 'second of angle' (1/60 of a minute of angle), so I'll use (') to represent minute of angle.
The value of an angle measure can be calculated for any distance from its origin, the center of the circle or the muzzle of the barrel. In the case of MOA, it is the center of the circle. Therefore, if a circle has a 6 inch radius, one minute of angle represents 0.1047 / 60 = 0.001745 inch at 6 inches from the center. The value of MOA at 100 yards is 1.047 inches (0.001745 x 600).

In the case of a firearm sighting scope, the distance covered by the arc is relative to the circumference of the circle containing it. If the radius of the circle is 6 inches, it is the same as the circumference of the circle. But, if the radius of the circle is 3 inches, it is 1/2 the circumference of the circle. If the radius of the circle is 1 inch, it is 1/6 the circumference of the circle, and so on.
So, when we use MOA in a firearm sighting scope, we must know the actual size of the circle to get the correct value. But, that's not all. We must also know the size of the click on the scope turret. Each click on the scope turret is usually 1/4 MOA, but on some scopes it is 1/8 MOA. So, if we have a scope with 1/4 MOA per click and four clicks, we have 1.047 inch change at 100 yards.
The real difference between inch and MOA is 0.47 inch at 1000 yards.

Then, make and record as many elevation clicks as keep the group on target without reaching the scope's adjustment limit, shooting at the same aiming point. Determine the center of the second group by the Average Group Radius method, then return elevation to its previous setting.
Divide the distance between the two group centers by the number of elevation clicks used to get group two; the result is the value of each click at that distance.

In the case of inch, we must know the distance and the inch measure to calculate it at other distances. For example, if a group measures 1 inch, that should be written '1 inch'. If a group measures 0.75 inch, that should be written '0.75 inch'. If a group measures 0.5 inch, that should be written '0.5 inch'.
If we use the word 'inch' in writing, we should always spell it out and not use the symbol ("). The symbol (") is inaccurate for inches in this context and misleading because it also represents 'second of angle' (1/60 of a minute of angle).
The above discussion is all well and good, but it isn't all that critical to most shooters. MOA is a pretty close approximation to the inch and, for practical purposes, it is close enough. But, not all scopes are precisely calibrated to MOA or to the inch. Some are pretty close, but not close enough. And, for serious target shooting and increasing distances, attention to the MOA value relative to sight adjustment becomes more essential. Knowing the actual value of each scope adjustment is wise, especially if settings are changed in the field.

Ontario has an ingrained barrier to experiential learning.
This week the Ministry of Education asked school boards to provide a “snapshot” of the fees they ask students to pay. It’s a reasonable request, given that the text books say more than 77 per cent of our schools charge an activity fee of some sort, but it’s a question that school boards can’t really answer.
They don’t have a handle on the fees that their students are asked to pay to explore talents outside the classroom. Indeed, the school boards themselves often don’t know these fees. A study in a school board that serves as a provincial barometer found membership in one school team could cost up to $455. And that was just the start.
The study showed a massive range of fees among different schools, even schools separated by a few blocks. The problem is that schools charge on a club-by-club basis with no central authority governing the amount charged. So, students who want to play volleyball and rugby could be looking at costs that approach $1,000. The start-of-term levy is just the first of a long litany of costs.

The ministry should then fund extracurricular activities in concert with non-profit groups and other ministries and phase out the fees. It’s not that the ministry doesn’t know these fees exist. It’s that it considers them “extras” over and above the basic education system. This is the problem.
Experiential learning is the difference between an engaged and a disengaged student. It can be the difference between children who are fighting obesity and those who are not.
School boards need to first figure out how much their students are asked to pay. Then, they should debate a motion, like the one set to take place at the Toronto District School Board, to provide a standard, board-wide fee as a first step on getting control of this issue. But there is more to be done.
The current definitions of what constitutes an “extracurricular activity” at the ministry level consider them an “extra.” They are an extra over and above the basic education system. This is a problem. Extracurricular activities can sometimes best be taught on the football field.

Hidden costs such as cellphone system-access fees and student-activity fees add to the price of cheap products and education. But the fees in schools, especially the ones that challenge poverty reduction and equity in education, are ones that should be removed from our schools.

Our brains don’t always store memories in the way we think they do. A recent study published in the journal Neuron examined the effect of curiosity on learning, and its findings were fascinating. Although we know that material that is interesting is easier to learn than material that is boring, the way our brains work when we’re curious is still mysterious. How curiosity affects memory is still unclear, but the authors of this study suggest that there may be a mechanism involving the release of dopamine, a neurotransmitter that’s already linked with learning and extrinsic reward.
What is extrinsic reward-related memory?
Extrinsic reward-related memory is learning that is related to rewards we receive from the outside world, like food or money. The reward in this task, having curiosity satisfied, comes from within. This study is important because it suggests that there may be a common mechanism shared between extrinsic and intrinsic reward-related memory, and gives the first major insight into the mechanisms of human memory.
The study
Henry Gustav Molaison (H.M.) was one of the most studied patients in neuroscience history. At age 27 H.M. underwent surgery to remove brain areas thought to cause epilepsy. Although the surgery worked well as a treatment for epilepsy, it caused severe anterograde amnesia. H.M. spent the next 50 years of his life in a steady present, unable to form new memories.
H.M. gave the first major insight into the mechanisms of human memory. Several experiments later showed that a structure within the medial temporal lobe region, the hippocampus, plays a key role in learning and memory. When two neurons are stimulated together multiple times, the strength of the electrical connection between them increases. This is called long term potentiation (LTP), and it is thought to underlie the formation of new associations and storage of new memories. The brain areas that have been previously linked to extrinsic reward-related memory were also activated when curiosity was increased.
In this study, the brain activity of each subject was monitored in an MRI scanner while a selected trivia question was presented, followed by its answer. The authors measured curiosity by asking subjects to rate how curious they were to learn the answer to each question. Before the answer appeared, subjects were shown a picture of a neutral face that was unrelated to the task. After the scan, participants were tested on their memory for the trivia answers and for the faces.
The results
Increased connection strength enhances the ability of neurons to transmit a signal. The authors found that curiosity improved participants’ memory for the trivia questions, and increased connection strength in the brain areas that have previously been linked to extrinsic reward-related memory. Increased connection strength also resulted in better memory for the faces shown after the questions.
In the brain scan, increased curiosity was associated with higher activation of the nucleus accumbens, substantia nigra, and ventral tegmental area. These brain areas have previously been linked to extrinsic reward-related memory, and the authors suggest that the mechanism may involve release of dopamine. Dopamine is a neurotransmitter that is already linked with learning and extrinsic reward.
Educators can take from this research the message: “Make it interesting, make me curious!” Material that is interesting is easier to learn than material that is boring, and this study shows why. Increased connection strength enhances the ability of neurons to transmit a signal, and this may underlie the formation of new associations and storage of new memories. Although how curiosity affects memory is still mysterious, this study shows that there may be a common mechanism shared between extrinsic and intrinsic reward-related memory, and drugs acting on the dopaminergic system could one day boost learning and memory by acting on the same circuits that boost learning of interesting material.

3D-printable polymer inks for medicine
Researchers at the University of Birmingham, UK, have developed biodegradable polymer inks that could be used to create surgical tools and custom-made prosthetics, as well as patient-specific organ replicas that surgeons can practise on before performing complicated operations. The team is now working on further animal studies with shorter and longer implant periods to observe the response across the material’s lifecycle.
Andrew Dove and his business partner, Andrew Weems, spun out 4D Medicine from the University of Birmingham to move the technology toward market approval. The two have developed polymer inks based on aliphatic polycarbonates that can be 3D printed into a support structure for tissue re-growth after tumour removal. As the scaffold degrades away, only natural tissue remains.
Weems was instrumental in developing the technology. As a PhD student, he contacted Dove about linking their experiences of 3D printing and shape memory, thinking the combination could have biomedical interest.
‘It was a big problem after breast cancer removal surgery, for example, you’ve got a big problem in the recovery,’ explains Dove. ‘It’s quite hard to reconstruct the tissue. That takes several operations.’
The team uses thiol-ene click chemistry to crosslink cyclic carbonate monomers and produce 3D polycarbonate structures that can be flexibly printed. By using multiple carbonate monomers, the researchers can produce resins with different mechanical properties when cured, such as a specific degradation rate. The resins are based on aliphatic polycarbonates – molecules that contain no aromatic groups between their carbonate linkages, making them less rigid than other polycarbonates.
Dove and Weems won the Royal Society of Chemistry’s Emerging Technologies competition in 2018 and went on to secure two rounds of funding to move the technology forward. In the first round, Dove and Weems won £50,000 in the Royal Society of Chemistry’s Emerging Technologies competition, and in the second, Weems was awarded a fellowship from the Whitaker International Program to work with Dove.
‘The big step we took is in the precise design of the monomer and the mixture of monomers that we used,’ Dove says. ‘That’s something that we’re still working on and it’s something that we can control. We can tune the properties of the material, and that’s a big advantage.’
Using thiol-ene chemistry to produce the inks avoids the potentially toxic residual acrylate groups that other biomaterial scaffolds rely on. Weems later received funding from Innovate UK’s Innovation and Commercialisation of University Research (Icure) scheme, financing researchers to explore the commercial potential of their research, to help the team take the final steps toward obtaining toxicology data to prove to regulators that the technology is safe.
‘I think the combination of the application we’re targeting, and the material we’re using will help mitigate that risk and the initial results really point us in the right direction,’ Dove says. ‘We can print any shape and size and we’ve got beautiful data that shows that there is no real reaction to these materials when they’re implanted. We can control its microstructure, its macroscopic shape, everything about it really, which is unusual.’
The team is now working on further animal studies with shorter and longer implant periods to observe the response across the material’s lifecycle. ‘The material can be used to fill the void where the tumour was,’ Dove says. ‘We can use it to help direct radiotherapy, and that will improve patient outcomes and survival rates.’
Dove sees the inks being used in paediatric applications, such as treating musculoskeletal problems. The bespoke printed products in different sizes will fit a child’s growing body more closely. ‘We can print any shape and size and we’ve got beautiful data that shows that there is no real reaction to these materials when they’re implanted,’ Dove says.
The team is also designing devices and trying to understand how they perform, but also how they feel and what patients would like from them. ‘We can control its microstructure, its macroscopic shape, everything about it really, which is unusual,’ Dove says. ‘We can tune the properties of the material, and that’s a big advantage.’
4D Medicine has 2 employees and is located in Birmingham, UK. The team is currently working on further animal studies with shorter and longer implant periods to observe the response across the material’s lifecycle.
The team has conducted a four month rat study on the material. ‘We’ve got a lot of work still to do to prove the safety of the material, and then there are lots of different steps we have to take along the road to get regulatory approval,’ Dove says. ‘Funding is always the biggest hurdle to developing a new technology, but we made very good progress very quickly and it became apparent that there was an opportunity to do something really impactful. Andrew coming in with a Whitaker fellowship was definitely a turning point in the story because it’s hard to get funding for an idea like this.’

This year, dairy health experts at the University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine’s New Bolton Center (NBC) have seen an increase in pneumonia cases. Many of these cases are in growing heifers and calves. The wide temperature swings and wet-warm weather in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic regions have contributed to this increase.
The first step to managing this disease is to implement the steps to prevent it from happening in the first place. The key to successful prevention of any disease is a good vaccination program. Vaccinations are a key component of disease prevention when used correctly. Producers should consult a veterinarian to find the best vaccine program for their specific operation, or have them develop a plan that is specific to the needs of their operation.
In addition to vaccinations, producers should also focus on air quality and air flow. Good ventilation significantly impacts the air quality and cooling capacity needed to prevent illness. Keeping curtains and windows open allows for good air flow. Producers on older farms should also consider installing a forced or tube installation system in their barns.
In addition to the steps listed above, producers should avoid or minimize additional sources of stress for their animals during the winter months. The stress of transporting animals, excessive intermingling, and bringing in new stock from outside sources or sale barns should be kept to a minimum if possible. Early recognition of illness is the key to success. Regularly monitoring animals, checking for signs of illness and taking temperatures of animals with symptoms helps recognize illness early and gives the best chance of effective treatment and prevention of long-term damage.
If an outbreak occurs, fast and aggressive treatment is the key to success. If producers are seeing a large number of animals affected with pneumonia, blanket treatments, including feed through antibiotics, can be effective. However, producers should always consult a veterinarian before using blanket treatments. If only a few animals are affected, the best course of action is to isolate those animals to help prevent the disease from spreading.
In summary, the key to successful prevention of this disease is to start with good ventilation and a solid vaccination program. Regularly monitoring animals, checking for signs of illness, and taking temperatures of animals with symptoms helps recognize illness early and gives the best chance of effective treatment and prevention of long-term damage. Finally, if an outbreak occurs, fast and aggressive treatment is the key to success.

Mental health is in shambles thanks to the pandemic. Governments are now dealing with the task of reviving the economy and reshaping acceptable social interactions, but the people are left to deal with the fallout. The routines that kept life in order are in shambles, and people are exercising less, binge-watching Netflix, and eating large amounts of junk food. There is a lot of free time because everyone is staying home, but realizing that it isn’t used well can cause anxiety about wasting it. News sometimes leans on sensationalism, and people can be affected by prevalent depressing news that they have no control over.
It is important to monitor physical condition because mental well-being and physical health are two sides of the same coin, body and mind. The pandemic has left both in shambles, and it shouldn’t be hopeless.
Tip 1: Understand the science behind stress
Stress is a normal body response, and it can be managed and even used to advantage. It is meant to shift the body into gear to deal better with precarious situations. Back about 200,000 years ago, if ancestors were facing a danger like a tiger in the dark, they would have pounding hearts and be sweating. These are manifestations of stress, and these stress responses are by design to shift the body into gear to deal better with precarious situations. When in danger, a quickened pulse and breathing, and increased muscle tension would indicate heightened alertness and brain activity. That is the brain hardwired to release oxytocin, serotonin, and dopamine, the trifecta of happiness, in response to altruism. Doing something that your future self will be proud of is encouraged.
Tip 2: Reduce media consumption
The 24-hour news cycle makes it easy to get overloaded with information. It is important to consume information that is reliable since the internet can be a muddle of semi-truthful content. The pandemic has been especially bad for the mental health of people without access to information in their primary language. According to the CDC, the pandemic has been especially bad for the mental health of people at higher risk for severe illness from COVID-19, such as older people and people of any age with certain underlying medical conditions. It has also been especially bad for the mental health of people caring for family members or loved ones, socially isolated people, such as people who live alone and people in rural or frontier areas, people with disabilities or developmental delay, people who use substances or have a substance use disorder, and frontline workers such as health care providers and first responders.
Many people would appreciate such help during the pandemic. The information consumed should be reliable, and limiting the times that mainstream news is consumed each day can help. It is important to understand the science behind stress. There are a lot of people who handle earth-shaking life changes, and there are others who get worked up over minutiae. Each person will respond differently to stress. The pandemic has been especially bad for the mental health of people in some racial and ethnic minority groups, and it has also been especially bad for the mental health of children and teens. It is important to understand the science behind stress because it can be managed and even used to advantage.
Tip 3: Do something you’ve always wanted to do
There is a lot of free time now that everyone is staying home, and it is important to realize that it isn’t used well. Doing something you’ve always wanted to do is encouraged. This could mean starting the first chapter of a book or crystallizing a long-contemplated business plan. It is important to take care of yourself. Be productive and get your mind off the virus. Doing something that your future self will be proud of is encouraged. According to Atticus in a poem, “Time is all we have and don’t.” It is very important to monitor physical condition. Mental well-being and physical health are two sides of the same coin, body and mind.
Tip 4: Help others
Giving is a powerful neural pathway to happiness. It is important to help others. This could mean helping with money or time, talents, and expertise.
